diagnosis.question: why was every HydraDB request ~45 ms, flat from 100 to 5,000 services?
diagnosis.cause: Per-request overhead in the client-to-published-port hop, not HydraDB and not graph work. HydraDB answers in 0.1 to 0.9 ms (server-side, from its /metrics histogram) and its response always arrives in one read. Clients that write the request headers and body separately (httpx, http.client, HTTP/2) took ~45 ms through Docker Desktop's published port on Windows; the same clients inside the docker network took 0.3 to 1.5 ms. A client that sends headers+body in ONE write took 0.4 ms through the same published port, and so did Bolt. Client-side TCP_NODELAY did not change it (so it is not simply the client's Nagle), which points at the proxy hop reacting to the split writes.
diagnosis.server_response_writes: 1 read per response (no header/body split), max gap between reads 0 ms
diagnosis.response_timing_fields: none in the HTTP response (columns, rows, read_epoch, next_cursor, bookmark); server timing comes from /metrics graph_client_operation_read_duration_seconds
diagnosis.transport_chosen: persistent HTTP/1.1 connection, one write per request (ghostwalk/graph/fasthttp.py): identical results (8 parity tests), 0.5 ms vs 45 ms per query; Bolt (~1 ms) was the alternative
also_fixed: the revision check is id-anchored (about 1 ms instead of 12 ms)
a graph read issues its independent queries together (about 40 ms instead of 85 ms)
diagnosis.not_transport: HydraDB writes still take about 22 ms each (server-side commit), and a scan filtered on a property such as `co` costs 11 to 50 ms server-side

scenarios.title: AWS us-east-1 DynamoDB disruption, 19 to 20 October 2025

source.title: Summary of the Amazon DynamoDB Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region (AWS)

scenarios.label: Replay built from the public postmortem; illustrative, not an accuracy measurement.
what_happened: A race between DynamoDB's DNS automation components (a planner that produces DNS plans and enactors that apply them to Route 53) left the regional DynamoDB endpoint with an empty DNS record (paraphrased from the post-event summary).
DynamoDB API calls failed; services that depend on DynamoDB (EC2's droplet workflow manager, Lambda, STS, IAM sign-in) degraded.
Later, EC2 launches, network configuration propagation and Network Load Balancer health checks were affected as a consequence.
assumptions: Dependencies are the ones the summary describes; the 'official map' is our construction of what a service catalog would list.
The invisible dependency is the control plane: a runtime dependency map shows services calling DynamoDB, not the automation that keeps DynamoDB's DNS record correct.
Alerts are in the order the summary describes the impact; their spacing is normalised (the real gaps were minutes to hours).

stages.stage: official map (the hidden dependency is missing)
after one postmortem teaches the edge (tentative)
after a second incident confirms it

llm.reason: DynamoDB is the deepest shared dependency in the topology and triggered the initial error_rate alert at +0s. All subsequent alerts in dependent services like lambda, ec2-dwfm, sts, and ec2-launch are downstream symptoms of the DynamoDB failure.

scenarios.title: Cloudflare outage, 18 November 2025
scenarios.label: Replay built from the public postmortem; illustrative, not an accuracy measurement.
what_happened: A change to database access controls in a ClickHouse cluster made a query that builds the Bot Management 'feature file' return duplicate rows, so the file roughly doubled in size (paraphrased from the postmortem).
The core proxy's Bot Management module had a limit on the file size that the doubled file exceeded; the proxy failed and customers saw HTTP 5xx errors.

Workers KV (its front-end gateway runs on the proxy), Access, Turnstile and dashboard login failed as a consequence; the status page also went down at the same time, which the postmortem says was a coincidence.
assumptions: Dependencies are the ones the postmortem describes; the 'official map' is our construction of what a service catalog would list.

The invisible dependency is the generated feature file: the proxy's Bot Management module loads a file that a separate job builds from a ClickHouse query and distributes network-wide. A service catalog lists the job's query on ClickHouse, not the file the proxy loads.
Alerts are in the order the postmortem describes the failures; their spacing is normalised (the real gaps were minutes).

stages.stage: official map (the hidden dependency is missing)
after one postmortem teaches the edge (tentative)
after a second incident confirms it

llm.reason: core-proxy is upstream of most failing services and its error_rate spikes before downstream services, indicating it as the primary source of the cascade.
